summary: Describes OAuth client authentication using mutual TLS with X.509 certificates, and certificate-bound access and refresh tokens. Authorization servers can bind tokens to the client's certificate, and protected resources can check that binding, so stolen tokens are less useful.

eli5.summary: A token tied to your own ID card is useless to a thief. This lets clients prove who they are with a certificate and tie tokens to it.

questions: how do certificate bound access tokens work
subtitle: Lets OAuth clients authenticate with TLS client certificates and ties access tokens to those certificates so stolen tokens are useless.

tldr.problem: An ordinary OAuth bearer token works for anyone who holds it, and shared secrets are a weaker way for clients to authenticate.
tldr.mechanism: The client uses mutual TLS with an X.509 certificate to authenticate to the authorization server, which can bind the issued access token to a hash of that certificate. The protected resource then checks that the certificate on its own TLS connection matches the binding.
tldr.outcome: A stolen or replayed access token cannot be used without the matching private key. Client authentication and token binding are separate and can be used independently.

today: RFC 8705 is a Proposed Standard, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It builds on RFC 6749 and RFC 7800.

sections.title: Introduction: Two Mechanisms for OAuth
sections.content:
In the basic OAuth 2.0 flow the client gets an access token from an authorization server and presents it to a protected resource, which validates it. This RFC adds two optional security mechanisms built on client-certificate mutual TLS: client authentication at the authorization server, and certificate-bound access tokens.

OAuth 2.0 defines shared-secret client authentication; mutual TLS offers better security characteristics. A bound token is a proof-of-possession token (also called key confirmation or holder-of-key), unlike a RFC 6750 bearer token, which any holder can use. Binding prevents use of stolen tokens and replay by unauthorized parties.

The two mechanisms are complementary but need not be deployed together. The mutual-TLS methods also apply to other endpoints that use client authentication, such as introspection and revocation. Mutual TLS here means the client sends its X.509 certificate and proves possession of the private key during the TLS handshake (the Certificate and CertificateVerify messages).
sections.eli5: Normally whoever holds the ticket gets in. Here the ticket is tied to your own ID card, and you show the card each time.

sections.title: Mutual TLS Client Authentication
sections.content:
This extends client credentials in RFC 6749. The authorization server decides, per client, whether mutual TLS is required. The TLS connection MUST have been established with mutual-TLS certificate authentication, and the client MUST include its client_id so the server can find the client's configuration and check the presented certificate against it. If no certificate is presented or it does not match, the server returns an invalid_client error.

There are two methods:

  • PKI method (tls_client_auth): the server validates the certificate chain and matches a single expected subject. A client registers exactly one of tls_client_auth_subject_dn, tls_client_auth_san_dns, tls_client_auth_san_uri, tls_client_auth_san_ip or tls_client_auth_san_email. Revocation checking is a deployment decision. A client can rotate its certificate by getting a new one with the same subject from a trusted CA.
  • Self-signed method (self_signed_tls_client_auth): the client registers its certificates through jwks or points to them with jwks_uri. The server does not validate the chain; the client is authenticated if the presented certificate matches a registered one. No PKI is needed, and with a jwks_uri the client can rotate certificates without changing data at the server.
sections.eli5: Instead of a password, the client shows an ID card. One way checks that a trusted office issued the card. The other way just checks the card against a list you gave the server beforehand.

sections.title: Certificate-Bound Access Tokens
sections.content:
When the client uses mutual TLS at the token endpoint, the authorization server can bind the issued access token to the client certificate in a way the protected resource can read. The RFC defines two: embedding the certificate hash in the token, or returning it through token introspection.

For JWT access tokens the hash goes in the cnf claim as the x5t#S256 member: a base64url-encoded SHA-256 hash of the DER encoding of the certificate, with trailing = padding omitted. For introspection (RFC 7662), the same cnf structure is a top-level member of the response.

When using the token, the client MUST use a mutually authenticated TLS connection with the same certificate used at the token endpoint. The protected resource MUST get the client certificate from its TLS layer and verify it matches the one tied to the token. If not, it MUST reject the request with HTTP 401 and the invalid_token error code.

Because a token is only presented after the TLS handshake finishes, the resource server must know in advance that mutual TLS is in use; the token cannot decide whether to ask for a certificate. The RFC makes no provision for renegotiation or post-handshake authentication.
sections.eli5: The server writes a fingerprint of your ID card on the ticket. At the door, the guard compares the fingerprint with the card you show. If they differ, you are turned away.

sections.title: Metadata, Public Clients and Endpoint Aliases
sections.content:
Two metadata parameters, both named tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens, signal support. In authorization server metadata (RFC 8414) it means the server can issue bound tokens; in client registration metadata it means the client intends to use them. Both are optional booleans that default to false. If such a client calls the token endpoint without mutual TLS, the server may return an error or issue an unbound token.

Public clients (those with no credentials tied to the client_id) can use bound tokens without mutual-TLS client authentication. Each client instance creates a self-signed certificate, and the server binds the token to it. If a refresh token is issued, the server SHOULD bind it to the certificate too.

Because requesting a client certificate can annoy conventional clients, especially browsers that show certificate pickers, a server may publish mtls_endpoint_aliases: alternative endpoints such as a token endpoint on a different host. A client that intends to do mutual TLS MUST use the alias when present.
sections.eli5: Even a guest without a membership card can get a ticket tied to a homemade ID. And the club may open a separate side door for people who show ID, so others are not bothered.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
An authorization server that supports mutual TLS alongside other methods or public clients would make client certificates optional. To support only the self-signed method, it would not check that the certificate was issued by a trusted CA. It may host the token endpoint on a separate host name or port to avoid affecting the TLS behavior of other endpoints such as the authorization endpoint.

The resource server relies on the authorization server for client authentication, so mutual TLS there is purely proof-of-possession. It does not need to validate the trust chain of the client certificate.

Because tokens are bound to a specific certificate, a certificate update invalidates them; the client handles that like an expired token by requesting a new one, typically with a refresh token. Binding of tokens issued from the implicit grant is out of scope, so use grants where the client calls the token endpoint directly, such as authorization code and refresh token. TLS may be terminated at a load balancer or proxy, but how the certificate details reach the application server is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Your ID card is tied to your ticket, so a new ID card means a new ticket. The club also decides which door does the checking.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Refresh tokens are already bound to the client by RFC 6749, so for clients using the mutual-TLS methods they are indirectly certificate-bound through the client ID. The thumbprint binding relies on SHA-256 having enough second-preimage resistance that another certificate with the same hash cannot feasibly be found. The RFC notes that security advice is a point-in-time statement.

With the PKI method, an attacker might use a certificate with the same subject issued by another CA the server trusts. The server SHOULD therefore accept only a limited number of CAs whose issuance policy meets its needs. Because X.509 parsing and validation is complex and mistakes have caused vulnerabilities, implementors SHOULD use an established X.509 library and SHOULD NOT write their own validation.

On privacy, before TLS 1.3 the client certificate is sent unencrypted in the handshake and could let third parties track and correlate activity. Clients acting for a single end user, such as a native mobile app, should use TLS 1.3 where possible.
sections.eli5: Be picky about which offices may issue ID cards, and use well-tested card readers instead of building your own. Older connections show your ID card to anyone watching, so use the newest kind.
